```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", warning = FALSE)
library(CloneCensorWeight)
```

`simulateCcwData()` generates synthetic OMOP-like cohorts with a
piecewise-exponential data-generating process, configurable confounding,
and a known true hazard ratio.  Because the truth is known, simulated data
are the right tool for three tasks:

1. **Validating the pipeline** — confirm the CCW estimate recovers the true HR.
2. **Demonstrating the role of IPCW** — show that skipping the weighting step
   introduces bias when confounding is present.
3. **Monte Carlo power analysis** — characterise operating characteristics
   (bias, RMSE, CI coverage, power) before running on real data.

---

# The data-generating process

## Parameters

| Parameter | Role |
|---|---|
| `treatmentPrevalence` | Marginal probability of treatment initiation |
| `trueHazardRatio` | True causal effect of treatment on the outcome hazard |
| `confoundingStrength` | How strongly the same covariates predict both treatment and outcome |
| `baselineHazard` | Baseline hazard per 30-day interval for an untreated subject with average covariates |
| `censorRate` | Loss-to-follow-up rate per interval |

The confounding mechanism is explicit: the same linear predictor that
drives treatment propensity also shifts the baseline hazard, so a naive
comparison will be biased whenever `confoundingStrength > 0`.

## Simulating a single dataset

```{r single-data}
set.seed(1)
dat <- simulateCcwData(
  n                   = 600,
  nCovariates         = 8,
  treatmentPrevalence = 0.45,
  trueHazardRatio     = 0.70,   # treatment reduces hazard by 30 %
  baselineHazard      = 0.025,
  censorRate          = 0.010,
  confoundingStrength = 0.70,
  gracePeriod         = 30,
  maxFollowUpDays     = 365,
  seed                = 1
)
```

```{r single-counts}
cohorts  <- dplyr::collect(dat$cohorts)
outcomes <- dplyr::collect(dat$outcomes)

cat(sprintf(
  "%d subjects | %d initiators (%.0f%%) | %d events (%.0f%%)\n",
  nrow(cohorts),
  sum(!is.na(cohorts$initiationDate)),
  100 * mean(!is.na(cohorts$initiationDate)),
  nrow(outcomes),
  100 * nrow(outcomes) / nrow(cohorts)
))
```

---

# Running the full CCW pipeline

```{r pipeline}
popArgs <- createCreateStudyPopulationArgs(
  riskWindowEnd                  = 365,
  endAnchor                      = "cohort start",
  removeSubjectsWithPriorOutcome = FALSE
)

cloneArgs <- createCreateClonesAndCensorArgs(
  arms = list(
    createArmDefinition("initiate", "initiateWithin", gracePeriod = 30),
    createArmDefinition("never",    "deferBeyond",    gracePeriod = 30)
  ),
  intervalLength = 30
)

createStudyPopulation(dat, outcomeId = 1L, popArgs)
cloned   <- createClonesAndCensor(dat, cloneArgs)
pt       <- discretizePersonTime(cloned, intervalLength = 30)
weighted <- createCensoringWeights(pt, cloned)
```

```{r weight-summary}
wSummary <- summary(weighted$weight[weighted$weight > 0])
print(wSummary)
```

The distribution of IPCW weights reflects how much re-weighting is needed
to restore balance.  Values far from 1 indicate stronger informative censoring.

```{r ccw-model}
modelArgs <- createFitOutcomeModelArgs("cox", "robust")
model_ccw <- fitOutcomeModel(weighted, fitOutcomeModelArgs = modelArgs)

s <- model_ccw$summary
cat(sprintf(
  "CCW estimate:  HR = %.3f  (95%% CI %.3f–%.3f)  p = %.3f\n",
  s$estimate, s$lower95, s$upper95, s$pValue
))
cat(sprintf("True HR: 0.700\n"))
```

---

# The role of IPCW: what happens without weighting?

Setting all IPCW weights to 1 is equivalent to a naive clone-only analysis
that ignores informative censoring.  With `confoundingStrength = 0.70`,
subjects who remain uncensored in each arm are a selected subset — and that
selection is not random.

```{r unweighted-model}
# Override weights to 1 — keeps the cloning structure, discards IPCW
pt_naive         <- weighted
pt_naive$weight  <- 1

model_naive <- fitOutcomeModel(pt_naive, fitOutcomeModelArgs = modelArgs)

sn <- model_naive$summary
cat(sprintf(
  "Naive estimate: HR = %.3f  (95%% CI %.3f–%.3f)  p = %.3f\n",
  sn$estimate, sn$lower95, sn$upper95, sn$pValue
))
```

```{r comparison-table}
comparison <- data.frame(
  Method    = c("CCW (with IPCW)", "Naive (weight = 1)", "Truth"),
  HR        = c(s$estimate,  sn$estimate, 0.700),
  Lower95   = c(s$lower95,   sn$lower95,  NA),
  Upper95   = c(s$upper95,   sn$upper95,  NA),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
knitr::kable(comparison, digits = 3,
             col.names = c("Method", "HR", "Lower 95%", "Upper 95%"),
             caption = "CCW vs. naive estimate. True HR = 0.70.")
```

The naive estimate is attenuated toward the null (or biased away from the
truth) because the covariates that drive treatment initiation also affect
outcome risk.  IPCW restores the intended comparison.

---

# Covariate balance

IPCW should also reduce covariate imbalance between the arms.

```{r balance}
smd_before <- computeStandardizedDifferences(dat)
smd_after  <- computeStandardizedDifferences(dat, weights = weighted)

cat("Max |SMD| before weighting:", round(max(abs(smd_before$smd)), 3), "\n")
cat("Max |SMD| after  weighting:", round(max(abs(smd_after$smd)),  3), "\n")
```

```{r love-plot, fig.width=6, fig.height=3.5}
if (requireNamespace("ggplot2", quietly = TRUE)) {
  plotLovePlot(smd_before, smd_after)
}
```

---

# Kaplan–Meier curves

```{r km, fig.width=6, fig.height=4}
if (requireNamespace("ggplot2", quietly = TRUE)) {
  plotKaplanMeier(weighted)
}
```

# Monte Carlo operating characteristics

`runSimulation()` automates repeated simulation and estimation so you can
characterise bias, RMSE, CI coverage, and power before running the analysis
on real data.

## Under the null (HR = 1): type I error

```{r null-sim, cache=FALSE}
sim_null <- suppressWarnings(
  runSimulation(
    nSims               = 25,
    n                   = 250,
    trueHazardRatio     = 1.00,
    baselineHazard      = 0.025,
    censorRate          = 0.010,
    confoundingStrength = 0.70,
    gracePeriod         = 30,
    seed                = 42
  )
)

summarizeSimulation(sim_null, trueHazardRatio = 1.00)
```

Coverage should be near 95% and power (= type I error here) near 5% when
the method is correctly calibrated.  With only 25 replications, Monte Carlo
error is substantial; production studies use ≥ 1 000.

## Under the alternative (HR = 0.7): power

```{r alt-sim, cache=FALSE}
sim_alt <- suppressWarnings(
  runSimulation(
    nSims               = 25,
    n                   = 250,
    trueHazardRatio     = 0.70,
    baselineHazard      = 0.025,
    censorRate          = 0.010,
    confoundingStrength = 0.70,
    gracePeriod         = 30,
    seed                = 42
  )
)

summarizeSimulation(sim_alt, trueHazardRatio = 0.70)
```

```{r sim-table}
null_summary <- summarizeSimulation(sim_null, trueHazardRatio = 1.00)
alt_summary  <- summarizeSimulation(sim_alt,  trueHazardRatio = 0.70)

results_df <- data.frame(
  Scenario        = c("Null (HR = 1.0)", "Alternative (HR = 0.7)"),
  Convergence     = c(null_summary$convergenceRate, alt_summary$convergenceRate),
  Bias            = c(null_summary$bias,            alt_summary$bias),
  RMSE            = c(null_summary$rmse,            alt_summary$rmse),
  Coverage        = c(null_summary$coverage,        alt_summary$coverage),
  Power           = c(null_summary$power,           alt_summary$power),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

knitr::kable(results_df, digits = 3,
             caption = paste("Operating characteristics from 25 replications",
                             "(n = 250 per replication). Increase nSims ≥ 1000",
                             "for production power analyses."))
```

## Estimate distribution

```{r estimate-dist, fig.width=6, fig.height=3.5}
if (requireNamespace("ggplot2", quietly = TRUE)) {
  conv_null <- sim_null[sim_null$converged, ]
  conv_alt  <- sim_alt[sim_alt$converged, ]

  plotData <- rbind(
    data.frame(logRr = conv_null$logRr, Scenario = "Null (HR = 1.0)"),
    data.frame(logRr = conv_alt$logRr,  Scenario = "Alt  (HR = 0.7)")
  )

  ggplot2::ggplot(plotData, ggplot2::aes(x = exp(logRr), fill = Scenario)) +
    ggplot2::geom_density(alpha = 0.4) +
    ggplot2::geom_vline(xintercept = c(0.70, 1.00),
                        linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
    ggplot2::scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0.2, 2.5)) +
    ggplot2::labs(x = "Estimated HR", y = "Density",
                  title = "Sampling distributions of the CCW estimator") +
    ggplot2::theme_minimal() +
    ggplot2::theme(legend.position = "bottom")
}
```

The dashed lines mark the true HRs.  The null distribution should be
centred on 1 (no bias); the alternative distribution should be centred on
0.7 and shifted left relative to the null, with overlap inversely
proportional to power.

---

# Guidance for production simulation studies

| Setting | Recommendation |
|---|---|
| `nSims` | ≥ 1 000 for stable power estimates; ≥ 500 for coverage |
| `n` | Match expected study size or sweep over a range |
| `confoundingStrength` | Calibrate to domain knowledge about the indication |
| `baselineHazard` | Set from published incidence rates for the outcome |
| `censorRate` | Set from observed loss-to-follow-up rates in pilot data |
| `fitOutcomeModelArgs` | Use the same settings as the planned real analysis |

Parallel execution is straightforward: split the `seed` range across
workers and `rbind()` the results.
